Content: Hey Wendover! The curious thing is, the tracks continue north from St. Albans, and the Vermonter line used to continue past St Albans and run all the way to Montreal Canada. Currently, the only line that goes to Montreal leaves from Penn Station in NYC, so if, for example, someone from Boston, MA (metro population approx. 5,000,000) wanted to take a train to Montreal (metro population 4.2 million), they would have to first travel south to NYC, stay overnight, then connect with the train to Montreal, for a total travel time of 25 hours. By car, the trip takes about 5 hours. Why does the Vermonter stop in St. Albans? Why doesn’t it continue up to Montreal?

Author: @nunyabidniz2868
Content:
Bottom line: a century ago, rail companies gave passenger trains priority, shunting freight off on a siding. Once freight became their primary profit center and the sidings weren't long enough for the huge consists they pulled to keep their cost/mile down, the passengers got stuck on sidings while freight rolled by, and ridership began to steadily decline. Because passenger rail service is still primary in Yurp [freight there still moves mostly by waterway, thanks to different geography and centuries of canal building before railways were invented], tickets prices and transit times are still reasonable.

Amtrak needs its own rails if it wants to remain viable, but they can't afford to secure the right of ways & build them.

Content: There are a couple of things kind of missing here.  I used to live in Milwaukee, and would go down to Chicago every 2 or 3 months.  Both stations are downtown, as are many, and both have good connection via local public transportation.  Obviously Chicago is better, but the various busses in Milwaukee are a benefit.  There is also the rise of companies like Uber/Lift that make getting to the station in Milwaukee easier as well.  Additionally, there is also the airports.  The Haiwatha line has a stop at Milwaukee International, and it usually is less expensive to fly out of than O'hare.  But O'hare has better flights, so flying out of there can be more convenient.  While I drove to Milwaukee International (usually), I also took the Haiwatha to Chicago and then the El to O'hare as well.  The point is that various kinds of local public transport, as well as thoughtful location of stations, are just as important.

Author: @uigrad
Content:
I used to think that Amtrak's only value was the jokes about government inefficiencies, or jokes about "the worst part of automobiles and planes combined."

Since moving to the NE, I've had the ability to try the NE corridor, and I can see the value now.  It's so much quieter and comfortable than flights, and the loading procedure is so much easier.   Unlike driving, I can read or work on a laptop instead of keeping my eyes on the road.  It really is the best of both.  If I'm going to a city where I can rely on a solid public transit system, there's no reason I wouldn't take the train.

Amtrak still has some growing to do.  Sometimes that sounds like a doctor telling an 89 year old that there body hasn't fully matured, but in this case, it really is true.  In an ideal world, it could be spun off again into one or more private services, but for that to happen, I think we'd have to make enormous changes to legislation, so that these companies could share infrastructure but still compete with each other.  And of course, profit would be absolutely necessary for that to happen, and we are long way from that as well.

Author: @ToABrighterFuture
Content:
Amtrak's problem is that a national network, requires national-level management.

And if who's running Washington changes mid-buildout, THEN what?

But to anyone who thinks having Democrats in charge, would be a cure-all for Amtrak, just look at how sapphire-blue Maryland builds its infrastructure, and imagine that on a national scale.

Some examples:

Route 200 sat on the drawing board for half a century, thanks in no small part to endless environmental litigation.  It wasn't until Paul Ehrlich, a rare Republican governor, basically told the environmentalists to sit down and shut up, that Route 200 finally got built.

Ever heard of the Hay's Spring amphipod?  Very few had, until its habitat was threatened by construction of the DC Purple Line.  Now, to be fair, that's not the only delay that project has encountered.  But it was one issue of many.  The Purple Line was slow to start construction, one contractor has already quit the project, the opening date has been pushed back by half a decade AND COUNTING, and it's already five billion dollars over budget.  For a 16.2 MILE LIGHT RAIL LINE.  That's an overrun that works out to over $300,000,000, per mile.  How many miles is it just from New York to Chicago?

The Silver Spring Transit Center was supposed to be a two year build.  It took seven.  And it quickly, and predictably, descended into an EDP magnet.  (And no, I *don't* mean perfume.)

The Key Bridge on 695 collapsed in March 2024.  Demolition of the old structure wasn't completed until the summer of 2025.  Think they'll have it open by December 2028?  Because if you do, then you don't know how awful Maryland is at building infrastructure.

Again, imagine all that, on a national scale, building a rail network.

But if you want to make an apples to apples comparison that's specific to choo-choos, then fine.  Brightline Florida went from proposal in March 2012, under Governor Rick Scott, to revenue service in January 2018, under Governor Ron DeSantis, Republicans both.  

California High Speed Rail broke ground in January 2015--I won't even *mention* how long it's been on the drawing board--and it is still under construction a decade later, with no revenue service in sight.

One theoretical solution would be, for Congress to authorize private rail carriers to go national, with expedited rights of way. 

But if Maryland is any indication, the environmentalists won't have any of it, despite the obvious interest rail carriers would have to keep the views as pristine as possible, AND despite the long-term environmental benefit of a more extensive rail network.

Pace 2:32 et seq., the Trump administration is not an existential threat to Amtrak.

Content:
The major bottleneck for Amtrak is the lack of rolling stock, especially when at some point they will have to retire the current fleet. They can't afford to just replace them 1 for 1. They're going to need a much higher count of cars if Amtrak is to expand.

For long distance trains, it really needs to be more than 1 train per day (or three times a week on routes like the Cardinal). For example, it is absolutely criminal for a city like Atlanta, GA to only have the Crescent heading towards NYC departing at 1130 at night and the waiting room is packed with people waiting for this train.

On top of that, what's hurting long distance trains is that instead of having a train ready to go at the terminal, they rely on the arriving train to immediately be serviced and turned around for the next trip out. This has always been highly problematic since long distance trains tend to be late and therefore the train leaves late going back the other way. They need a spare factor that doesn't rely on doing this.

Author: @leeharrison2722
Content:
I ride Amtrak back and forth from Albany NY to NYC several times a month.  This is one of the most heavily used lines in the country, and one that ought to at least not lose money.  The service is OK, too ... nothing to really complain about ... but its a bit slow, and often a bit late.

Every few years the state government in Albany commissions a new "high speed rail" study -- spending money on consultants.  The results never change, because reality doesn't change: the right-of-way up the Hudson river won't support high speed rail.  If you want high-speed rail it needs to be moved off the banks of the river ... and the logical route parallels the NY Thruway.  This would require major investments ... the only thing about the study that changes is the numbers just go up.   The shifted route would also have major consequences for the towns on the east side of the Hudson ... that have a long-enduring love/hate relationship with the railroad.   In many ways they'd be left with the worst of it: the freight traffic would remain, and the value of being able to catch a train in your own small town would be gone.

I realist sees that high-speed rail simply won't happen to Albany and points north.  At least the state could admit that?

Author: @anthonyyen5807
Content:
There are no large scale (nation-spanning), continuously-profitable passenger rail inter-city systems that took and currently take zero public subsidies of any form for infrastructure (tracks, stations, etc.), operations, maintenance, and capital, across the entire world.

Even the US freight rail system held up as an icon of rail capitalism was founded on historic land grants by the federal government, takes Consolidated Rail Infrastructure and Safety Improvements (CRISI) Grant Program funds for regional and short-line track and infrastructure projects, and takes federal government funds projects to eliminate or improve the safety of highway-rail grade crossings.

Highways’ operating costs, maintenance and acquisition are also not fully covered by the freight trucking industry. Depending upon whose calculations you use, the trucking industry only pays for between 40-60% of its actual costs upon the roadways system. Nobody disputes that the trucking industry is subsidized in some manner, the arguments are over the degree of subsidy.

Author: @Plasmawarrior
Content:
This video has one major problem: It assumes that either Trump or Biden are responsible for the success or failure of Amtrak. Neither has done much to get in the way as we know it.  However, don't think Amtrak alone is the main cause of their success. Airlines are also doing their part to make things worse. Southwest is a prime example. Sure, Amtrak isn't amazing, but it's somewhat steady, which is helping itself out just a bit more than anything else.

...But there's still a lot that it isn't fixing, nor seems to want to. I just went from Laurel, Mississippi to Houston, Texas. And while I could get on the Amtrak train from Laurel to New Orleans in 4 hours, the trip from New Orleans to Houston on Amtrak would have taken almost 2 days. While a Greyhound took 7 hours. And while that may still be longer than flying, it's still much better than the cost of driving myself. Amtrak needs to do better with its hub locations everywhere, not just in the Northeast. One great lakes train improvement isn't really enough; even if that is 1% better, it isn't good enough for most of the country.

Author: @brucehain
Content: The more gentle cut-and-cover routing from the 1930s, as drawn by the PRR would have been the correct alternative. That's why they chose the longer, more circuitous option: it costs more to build. A competent and creative attempt to build the correct alignment would certainly have been in order: with a basic rule being that anyone negatively affected by the work could expect compensation in the form of improvements to their properties, as a first priority. (looking at Street View you can see how there's a lot of room for improvement - in that way you could make the new tunnel a boon for everyone) The present boondoggle (that's intentional) will eventually be good for freight and non-NEC passengers, as the circuitousness doesn't matter so much with freight, and there's no other way to serve certain passenger destinations. I'm sure if anyone's read this far they will find the following an improbable idea, but to move the main station to Canden Yards is about the best location for brevity and unskewed headings you're likely to get. Involving orders of magnitude more tunneling than the present boondoggle, I can hardly see why it should cost $6,000,000,000 in 2025 dollars. That's bullshit.

Author: @adamperdue3178
Content:
I live in Virginia.  Around 2010 or so, it took about 20-24 hours to get from my town to D.C. (a 4 hour drive for comparison).  Around 2020, it was down to about 14 hours, and now on average it's a 10 hour trip.  (Keep in mind it's not a direct route to get to DC on Amtrak's route, it's a bit meandering so it's never going to be faster than driving)

10 hours still sounds like a very unreasonably long amount of time, and I wouldn't take that if I could avoid it as it's 250% the time it takes to drive...  But for people who either don't have a car or don't want to drive?  10 hours is very much a manageable trip.  I used to work with a man who moved to my town from DC who didn't have a car.  He walks to work every day (or sometimes people give him a ride), and he walks to the train station and hops on the Amtrak back to D.C. when he's got a few days off and goes to see his family.  Keep in mind this is a small town of 2,000 people in the middle of Appalachia, we're not in a major urban center, or even along the route between major urban centers.

The way I figure, if even rural Virginians in the middle of nowhere can have reasonable access to rail travel, then I figure the state as a whole must be having a massive Rennaisance in rail at the moment.

Content:
It's hard to understate just how much the freight companies are screwing up passenger rail. Beyond the delays from blocking passenger rail (which is supposed to be illegal), Amtrak is forced to run on their tracks for much of the country. The freight companies are absolute cheap-asses and won't pay for higher quality tracks, which means amtrak is forced to move at a glacial pace in many parts of the country. This may surprise people but those old amtrak trains that you see puttering along outside the NEC, can actually go anywhere from 100 MPH to 125 MPH.

If Congress could force these freight companies to upgrade their tracks, and if Amtrak was allowed to sue the freight companies for breaking the law, you could see a massive boost in speeds without needing to upgrade the rolling stock at all.

Author: @perhapsme988
Content:
Watching from Australia.

Here, we don’t have an actual functional NATION-wide passenger rail service. There is a federal agency but they are office people as it were.

Our states run their own long distance rail services as well as all the Suburban and regional services.

That is, the states are the owners and operators of all rail services within their state. 

The exception is some of the freight train services. They however do not own the tracks at all. The state owns the track. (some mining regions remote from anywhere have their own rail owned and run by mining companies) 

The federal agency has a rail infrastructure corporate that helps to maintain some rail tracks outside major population regions but not all of them and with the input of the state department. 

Municipalities do not run their rail at all. Indeed, even private local bus services far from population centres need to get licenses from the state transport department. 

All suburban rail and bus services are controlled and run directly (rail) and either directly or indirectly (bus) by the state transport department.

Our states tend to be huge in area- most are bigger than Texas. 

However most of the rail tracks outside state capitals tend to be used for agriculture and mining industries far more than passenger services . Freight trains too take up bulk of service runs too. 

Australia as a whole and in all states are sparsely populated. Outside capital cities of each of the states, population is small. Eg, my state of NSW, our capital city of Sydney has a larger population than the rest of the state which isn’t that much smaller than Texas.

Sydney has a large suburban rail service with over 300 stations. Sydeny is a very large metropolitan in area term. Melbourne too has a huge suburban rail network. They are all run by their reductive state government rail authorities. 
 
Our states also run their REGIONAL passenger services. Bulk of these are within 100 miles of their capital cities. 

Eg, Sydeny (my city) has several regional rail services. Newcastle/Central Coast is just under 90 miles from Sydeny Central Station. Blue Mountains line about 110m. Illawarra or South Coast line about 100m from Sydeny Central station. The Southern Highland (it has a diesel set whereas other regional lines have electric motor) is about 130miles.

All except Southern Highlands line has at least hourly service and all have other services but shorter distance. This is so even on weekends. Southern Highlands have lot fewer services because its destination area is never regarded as part of the greater Sydeny coverage. 

All these regional services are very good. 

Some ultra long regional services have their own train sets and are organised differently from shorter regional services. 

Our interstate rail services are run by individual states. However in effect there is only my state of NSW that runs such between Sydeny to Melbourne (state of Victoria) and Sydeny to Brisbane (Queensland). Indeed the other 2 states don’t put up a cent for it. They just let our trains run on their tracks.

We have other interstate services . Indian Pacific between Sydeny and Perth in Western Australia, the Ghan from Adelaide in South Australia to Darwin in Northern Territory, and the Overland between Melbourne and Adelaide are run by a private company. They are EXPENSIVE tourist services that basically are food fest. Often there are more overseas tourists than Aussies on these services.

The Indian Pacific and the Overland used to be run by state governments with subsidies from the federal government. Without federal government assistance, they were privatised.

I think Amtrak is in a difficult situation altogether.

Content:
The joy that was felt when the Corridor got more trains! I used to take them frequently about a decade ago and so often it was standing room only! People literally sat on their bags in the wheelchair sections because the trains had been overbooked assuming people wouldn’t show. This was especially true during back to school, any school holiday, and at the end of term. Students simply don’t have cars when attending colleges in Boston, Cambridge, Providence, NYC, Philadelphia, etc and they also don’t have them if they’re at the Coast Guard Academy and few have them if they’re at Sub School at the Groton Sub Base. I remember so many trains just packed with students! The trains are also the most efficient way to get into NYC for plays or concerts if you live in Philadelphia or nearby, so the trains were often packed on the weekends too. 
And now, even though I have a car I love, when I visit family solo in CT (I live near Philly) I don’t have to drive anymore because I can get a train and I have access to a car up there. It works out so well! When we visit as a family (bringing pets) we drive and 95 is decidedly less congested until you hit Connecticut. CT could really do to beef up their commuter rail. I’d also love to see PA do like Virginia has done and what the Chicago to St. Paul has done and connect Philly to Harrisburg to Pittsburgh and make sure to hit the big colleges on the way. It costs way too much to drive across PA on the toll road, but taking the train and getting to read a book sounds wonderful!

Author: @rzeqdw
Content:
I don't expect a productive response, but I'm hoping for one anyway

5:00 If rail transit service is so critical, why can't it make a profit? 

A lot of people like to criticize companies for being profit-seeking, and there are sure some companies that are defecting against society for short term profit. But the opposite of profit, is loss, and if you lose money every year, your service is not sustainable. Full stop. 

However much a train service costs to operate, is what it's going to cost to operate. The money to operate it has to come from somewhere, if it doesn't, it stops operating. "Operating for profit", among other things, just means that the people who benefit from the service are the ones who have to pay for it. The alternative, in the context of transit, is the government paying for it. But "The Government" is just what we call it when we all work together. So, one of two things must be true:

1) If the people riding the trains cannot afford to pay what it costs to operate trains out of their own pockets, then it doesn't magically become affordable if the government intermediates that process.
2) When the government intermediates that process, they're taking money from people who will not use the train, to subsidize it for people who will. 

if (1) is true, then that means fundamentally that getting government funding is just lighting money on fire, and this service will eventually collapse no matter what we do, and the more funding it gets, the bigger crater will be. If (2) is true, then there needs to be an accounting for how this is fair. Why should someone who doesn't ride the train pay the train fare for someone who does? Why shouldn't it go the other way around? We could just as easily live in a world where riding the bus is taxed to subsidize gasoline, but we don't. Why is one better than the other

(Note that, speaking personally, I can think of some very good reasons to give and am happy to say "2 is true, but, you should subsidize it. It's better for you, as well as them". But nobody's actually saying that. 

So, the question remains: if the people who use the train system can't or don't value it enough to pay what it costs to operate it, why should we keep operating it?

Author: @jonathanstensberg
Content:
The Borealis demonstrates the importance of the long-distance trains. Because the existence of the Empire Builder, the tracks and stations were able to accommodate the regional train with just a few cheap and quick upgrades. This made it possible to persuade the notoriously rail-hostile Wisconsin legislature to fund their portion of the upgrades. Without the long-distance train, the corridor would have required massive upgrades, the costs would have been enormous, Wisconsin would not have funded the project, and Borealis would have never happened.

Crucially, the long-distance trains are fully supported by Amtrak’s federal funding. This means that Amtrak can launch long-distance services on corridors that would never get passed skeptical and hostile legislatures. Once these long-distance services are running on upgraded corridors, it will be much easier to convince legislators to pitch in for minor upgrades to support regional services similar to the Borealis.

Content: I’m amazed to find out that Amtrak is growing, because it really is the worst of all worlds. I understand it’s because of government hamstringing, but I don’t understand why anyone would choose it as it currently exists. I live in a rural area and the nearest large airport is two hours away. It is cheaper and faster for me to buy a round trip plane ticket, drive two hours to the airport, pay for my week’s parking or however long, then drive two hours back when I come home than it is to ride the Amtrak. And what would be 5 hours one-way to combine my driving, boarding, and flying time is about 24 hours on an Amtrak. About double the cost and 5 times the amount of time for a very slight boost in convenience. And for even cheaper, I could take a greyhound or something on the same route that would take maybe 12 hours. Or, even cheaper than that, I could drive myself in about 8 hours. When it comes to medium-long distance travel, Amtrak is the slowest and most expensive option, and they have the fewest options, for only a bit more comfort. Once a week at like 4am an Amtrak headed to the east coast passes through, but I can catch one of dozens of planes going every day at all hours, or one of a handful of greyhounds every week. I’ve been on the trains of a handful of European countries and they were all reasonably priced and basically broke even with flying in total time by the time you go through security and wait for takeoff and whatnot, while being much more convenient and comfortable

Author: @WhatsOnTheOtherEnd
Content:
I’m incredibly thankful that my semi-regular travel to and from DC can be done entirely on American steel the whole way. I’ve seen rail systems across the world, and while the combination of the NYC subway, Acela, and DC Metro is far from world class, it’s been pretty reliable and each time I’m taking it I’m seeing signs of continued improvement and investment. On paper it isn’t a “big win” but it will be. I anticipate I’ll continue to be traveling this route for many years to come, and I’m excited to start rolling over the new projects that are being put into place. 

I can hope that if there’s only one thing we can learn from and fully embrace from the rest of the world, it is CONTINUED investment and construction for rail transportation. If we stop after knocking out a project or two, all the momentum is lost and we won’t see the efficiency gains we could be realizing. Rail costs a lot, but if we just keep doing it across the country, the costs will drop and the quality will get better.

Author: @tibbers3755
Content:
How amtrak gotten this far is quite something to note as an underdog, specially given how even the US govt was sublty trying to make it unsuccessful. The first line of locomotives built for Amtrak, The SDP40F was made so that if Amtrak did cease operation, the locomotives could easily be converted to freight operations.  Stacking up against them was:

The US since the 50s has been built up and changed, so that public transport, short of airplanes, is lackluster and ineffective, and in most places, near non-existent (heavy railroads rely on good last-miles connections via bus, local light, and metro heavy rail to stay a viable option against automobiles). 
Speaking of, automobiles were on the rise, for short and medium range transport for convenience and cost, while airlines had pure speed, taking away potential customerbase. 
The fallen flags (many of whom folded their passenger services into Amtrak) went bankrupt or merged in a bid of survival, forming the 5 (soon 4?) major Class I lines ( NS-UP, CSX, BNSF, CPKC) which are exlusively freight. 
What was left of the infrustructure was worn and still in shambles after extensive use during the two world wars, and with no return on investment into said wars hindered the safety and speed of early amtrak trains which were literally fast passenger equipment, dating from the 50s but sometimes even further back (looking at you, PRR Class GG-1). 
And a lot of societal changes also skewed things even further against them.
And yet, amtrak has weathered more than 50 years of the aftermath of the fall of North American Railroads, and still managed to expand, with potentially more routes on the way. Communities now are pooling money to look into getting a PGH-CHi via Fort Wayne line, Ohio is looking into expanding. Mardi Gras and Borealis are going strong in their respective regions. As a person who uses AMTK as my primary mode of travel, I hope to see more services and better existing services come about.

Author: @TheLiamster
Content:
My dream is for Amtrak to lead a national comprehensive rail expansion but that would require rail nationalisation which would probably never happen. The fact that America used to be one of the global pioneers in steam railways yet has fallen so far behind is shocking but also really sad. The good news is public support remains at all time high and the US it absolutely can and should invest in large scale infrastructure projects once again. 

For starters (and relating specifically for Amtrak) we need at minimum twice daily service on all routes on long distance routes, hourly service on intercity routes and half hourly on regional routes using clock faced scheduling (which is the basis for any rail transit in a developed country) with more trains running on public holidays, sports events and during peak hours. The path forward from there could be new (potentially HSR) routes, bringing back former routes so long as it’s possible to reuse existing or former ROW (or buying track ownership rights from freight railroads) to cut down on new tracks, electrification so EMU’s (or just electric locomotives) can be run on routes (probably starting with regional ones as it’s cheaper and Caltrain’s electrification project can serve as a model to implement best practices) providing the obvious benefits of lower pollution and noise (this saves on fuel and maintenance costs too), or better integrating with local and regional transit services (by directly serving airports or implementing through running). 

Simple (albeit expensive) things can also be done to boost overall ridership like offering new onboard amenities, promoting TOD (transit oriented development), partnering with airlines to sell combined “air rail” tickets (something Europe has mastered), offering steep discounts (especially on holidays) for the elderly, disabled and low income families and even providing free parking at stations (the last one would be controversial as transit enthusiasts hate so called “park and ride” stations). I know all this sounds optimistic but it is definitely possible even it’s a dream for a train enthusiast like me
